summary.title: The Mystery Baton of Col du Fer

public.title: The Mystery Baton of Col du Fer

statement.final: At the summit hut atop the Col du Fer, the relay marshals have racked up 25 team batons, all looking utterly identical. But one sneaky baton is an impostor: it's ever so slightly heavier or lighter than the rest (nobody knows which), while all 24 genuine batons weigh exactly the same. The hut keeps only a tiny two-pan balance for weighing them: each pan can hold at most 2 batons at a time, and the scale only gives a sensible reading when both pans carry the same number of batons — so every weighing must be either 1 baton against 1, or 2 against 2. Each time you weigh, the balance simply tells you which side is heavier, or that the two sides are equal. You get to decide each new weighing after seeing the outcomes of all previous ones. Your job is only to pinpoint which single baton is the impostor — you don't need to figure out whether it's heavier or lighter than the others. Assuming you play as cleverly as possible and the batons are arranged in the worst possible way against you, what is the fewest number of weighings that will always guarantee you can identify the faulty baton? Give your answer as an integer.
statement.original: The Col du Fer relay ends at a summit hut where 25 team batons are stored. Exactly one baton is defective: it weighs slightly more, or slightly less, than a genuine baton (which of the two is unknown). All genuine batons weigh exactly the same, and all 25 look identical. The hut's balance is tiny: each pan holds at most 2 batons, and a reading is meaningful only when both pans hold the same number of batons, so every weighing is 1-vs-1 or 2-vs-2. Each weighing shows which pan is heavier, or that they balance. You may choose each weighing after seeing the previous results. You must identify the defective baton (you need not say whether it is heavy or light). What is the smallest number of weighings that guarantees success in the worst case? Give your answer as an integer.

hints.text: Think about what a balanced weighing versus a tipped weighing each tell you, and notice that since only 2 batons can sit on each pan, a balanced result can only ever clear at most 4 batons from suspicion at a time — while a tip leaves you with a trickier situation, since you won't yet know whether a heavy-looking or light-looking baton is really the culprit.

Define $F(k)$ as the maximum number of totally unknown suspects (could be heavy or light) that you can always resolve in $k$ weighings once you have genuine reference batons available. Work out $F(1)$ and $F(2)$ directly by thinking hard about what outcomes are distinguishable, then find a recursion for $F(k)$ in terms of $F(k-1)$.

Show that $F(1)=2$ and $F(2)=5$ (not the naive 3 and 7 you'd get from purely counting balanced-weighing eliminations), and then argue that for $k\ge 3$, $F(k)=F(k-1)+4$ since a 2-vs-2 tip always leaves exactly 4 direction-known suspects that two further weighings can finish off. Compute $F(3),F(4),\dots$ up to enough weighings to see when $F(k)$ first reaches or exceeds the pool size left after the very first weighing.

Since your very first weighing (with no genuine baton yet available) can be balanced or tipped, a balanced result leaves $25-4=21$ totally unknown suspects. Compare $21$ to the sequence $F(5), F(6), \dots$ you computed: find the smallest $k$ with $F(k)\ge 21$, then add the one weighing already used to get the total number of weighings needed, and check that one fewer is provably impossible.

public.title: The Sore Mountain Marshals

statement.final: High in the mountains, a relay baton begins its journey at Hut 1, nestled in the northwest corner of a 4×4 village grid of huts numbered 1 through 16 in reading order (so Hut 4 sits at the northeast corner and Hut 16 at the southeast). The baton must reach Hut 16, and at every handoff the runner may only carry it one hut east or one hut south — so its whole journey touches exactly seven huts. Every hut has a marshal stationed at it. A marshal whose hut the baton actually visits is scrupulously honest and always tells the truth; a marshal whose hut gets skipped is left grumpy and sore, and always lies out of spite. After the relay finishes, four marshals give their statements: Marshal 6 claims, "Hut 11 was on the route." Marshal 7 insists, "Hut 5 was on the route." Marshal 10 declares, "Hut 3 was on the route." And Marshal 12 states, "Hut 2 was on the route." It turns out exactly one possible route through the grid makes all four statements consistent with the truth-telling and lying rules. Find that route, and report the sum of the numbers of its seven huts. Give your answer as an integer.
statement.original:
A mountain relay runs across a 4×4 grid of huts numbered 1–16 in reading order (1 = northwest, 4 = northeast, 16 = southeast). The baton starts at hut 1 and finishes at hut 16; each handoff carries it one hut east or one hut south, so its route passes through exactly seven huts. Every hut is staffed by a marshal: a marshal whose hut the baton visits always tells the truth, while a marshal whose hut is skipped is sore and always lies. Afterward, four marshals speak:
• Marshal 6: "Hut 11 was on the route."
• Marshal 7: "Hut 5 was on the route."
• Marshal 10: "Hut 3 was on the route."
• Marshal 12: "Hut 2 was on the route."
Exactly one route is consistent with all four remarks. What is the sum of the numbers of its seven huts? Give your answer as an integer.

Give your answer as an integer.

hints.text: Think about what it means for a marshal's statement to be 'consistent with the truth-telling rule': a marshal's honesty status is tied directly to whether their own hut is on the route.

Notice that each statement becomes a biconditional: marshal at hut X says hut Y was visited, and this is true exactly when 'hut X on route' matches 'hut Y on route' — so each pair (6,11), (7,5), (10,3), (12,2) must be both-visited or both-skipped.

Convert huts to grid coordinates and check the pair (3,10): since the route only moves east or south, see whether both could ever appear together — this should pin down that this particular pair must be skipped entirely.

With hut 3 and hut 10 ruled out, work through the two cases for pair (5,7) — 'both visited' or 'both skipped' — tracing the forced path each time to see which one avoids a dead end, then follow that surviving path all the way from Hut 1 to Hut 16, and add up the seven hut numbers you pass through.

public.title: The Fair Pizza Puzzle

statement.final:
At Mario's Perfectly Fair Pizzeria, every pie is cut only with straight slices that pass right through the center, spaced evenly apart, so every slice is exactly the same size. Tonight's pizza was cut into somewhere between 8 and 24 slices, inclusive. Three hungry friends—Ana, Ben, and Cleo—each make two guesses about the number of slices, and, true to their mischievous nature, each friend gets exactly one guess right and one guess wrong.

Ana says: "The number of slices is a multiple of 3," and also, "There are at least 20 slices."

Ben says: "The number of slices is a multiple of 9," and also, "The number of slices is a multiple of 4."

Cleo says: "The number of slices is a multiple of 6," and also, "There are fewer than 15 slices."

Given that exactly one statement from each friend is true and the other false, how many slices does the pizza have? Give your answer as an integer.
statement.original:
A round pizza was sliced so that every cut is a straight line straight through the center, with the cuts equally spaced — so all slices are identical and the split is perfectly fair. The total number of slices is between 8 and 24, inclusive. Three friends each make two claims, and each friend makes exactly one true claim and one false claim.

Ana: "The number of slices is a multiple of 3." / "There are at least 20 slices."
Ben: "The number of slices is a multiple of 9." / "The number of slices is a multiple of 4."
Cleo: "The number of slices is a multiple of 6." / "There are fewer than 15 slices."

How many slices were there? Give your answer as an integer.

hints.text: Think carefully about what it means for a slice to be cut by a straight line through the center — what does that force about the total number of slices?
Since every cut through the center produces two slices at once, the total slice count must have a special parity; use this to narrow down the range 8–24 before checking the friends' statements.

List the even numbers from 8 to 24, then for each friend's pair of statements, eliminate candidates where both statements are true or both are false — this trims the list down to just a few possibilities.

After eliminating with Ana's and Ben's statements, only a few numbers remain (like 12, 18, 20); apply Cleo's two claims (multiple of 6 / fewer than 15) to see which single candidate makes exactly one of her statements true.

public.title: Captain Vex's Even Split

statement.final: Captain Vex's crew has buried one doubloon at every lattice point (a point where both coordinates are integers) that lies strictly *inside* the convex quadrilateral whose corners are (0,0), (18,6), (14,20), and (-2,10), taken in that order around the shape. Doubloons resting exactly on the boundary edges don't count — the crew only trusts what's safely hidden within. When it comes time to split the loot, the port watch insists on claiming every buried doubloon whose two coordinates add up to an even number, while the starboard watch takes everything else. How many doubloons does the port watch collect? Give your answer as an integer.
statement.original: Captain Vex's crew buries one doubloon at every lattice point (both coordinates integers) lying strictly inside the convex quadrilateral with vertices (0,0), (18,6), (14,20), and (-2,10), listed in order. Lattice points on the boundary get no doubloon. At the split, the port watch claims every buried doubloon whose two coordinates sum to an even number, and the starboard watch claims all the rest. How many doubloons does the port watch receive? Give your answer as an integer.

hints.text: Think about counting all the buried doubloons first, using a tool that relates area, boundary points, and interior points of a lattice polygon.

Apply Pick's theorem to the quadrilateral to get the total interior count, then think about how to isolate just the points with even coordinate sum — notice these points form a sublattice that's itself a nice grid.

Compute the quadrilateral's area via the shoelace formula and its boundary count via gcd's of edge differences, then use the substitution $u=\frac{x+y}{2},\,v=\frac{x-y}{2}$ to map the even-sum points onto a new integer lattice polygon.

Find the images of the four vertices under this substitution (they'll be integer points since all vertex coordinate sums are even), compute the new polygon's area and boundary lattice count, and apply Pick's theorem once more to that transformed shape to finish.

summary.title: The Case of Mrs. Alvar's Flowerbed

public.title: The Case of Mrs. Alvar's Flowerbed

statement.final: Mrs. Alvar is redesigning her garden, and one bed is shaped like a perfect right triangle, with all three side lengths coming out to whole numbers of meters — a fact she's rather proud of. She's had her gardener lay a gravel path tracing all three edges of this triangular bed, and by the time he's finished, he reports that the path measures exactly 144 meters in total, matching the triangle's perimeter precisely. While admiring the work, the gardener also notices something curious: the hypotenuse of the bed is exactly 2 meters longer than the longer of the two legs. Mrs. Alvar, always one for a good puzzle, wonders how much space this flowerbed actually takes up. Can you help her figure out the area of the flowerbed, in square meters? Give your answer as an integer.
statement.original: In Mrs. Alvar's garden, one flowerbed is shaped like a right triangle whose three side lengths are whole numbers of meters. A gravel path runs along all three sides of this bed, and the path's total length (the triangle's perimeter) is exactly 144 meters. The gardener notes that the hypotenuse is exactly 2 meters longer than the longer leg. What is the area of the flowerbed, in square meters? Give your answer as an integer.

hints.text: Think of the garden bed's three whole-number sides as a Pythagorean triple, and translate the two clues (perimeter and hypotenuse-leg relation) into algebraic conditions on those sides.
Let the two legs be $a<b$ and set $c=b+2$; use the perimeter equation to express $a$ in terms of $b$, then plug into the Pythagorean theorem to get a single equation in $b$.
Substituting $a=142-2b$ into $a^2+b^2=(b+2)^2$ simplifies to $a^2=4(b+1)$, which leads to a quadratic $b^2-143b+5040=0$ — solve this quadratic to find the valid triangle's leg lengths.

Once you find the two integer solutions for $b$, discard the one that makes $a$ negative, and use the remaining valid leg lengths (with the hypotenuse from $c=b+2$) to compute the area via $\tfrac12 a b$.

public.title: The Circle of Suits

statement.final: A traveling magician arranges 20 playing cards face up on 20 numbered marks spaced evenly around a circular mat, like the hours of a very generous clock. Every card is either a heart, a spade, or a club, and only the suit pattern matters — two arrangements are considered different if even a single mark shows a different suit than before (spinning or flipping the mat doesn't make two layouts the same; each of the 20 marks is fixed and distinct). Walking around the circle in order, the magician groups the cards into maximal runs of consecutive matching suits, allowing a run to wrap around from mark 20 back to mark 1. Her one unbreakable rule of showmanship: every such run must contain exactly 2 or exactly 3 cards — no more, no less, and never a lonely single card. How many distinct suit arrangements on the 20 marks satisfy her rule? Give your answer as an integer.
statement.original: A magician lays 20 cards face up on 20 numbered marks evenly spaced around a circular mat. Each card is a heart, a spade, or a club; only the pattern of suits matters (two layouts are the same exactly when every numbered mark shows the same suit, so rotations and reflections count as different layouts). Reading around the circle, break the layout into maximal blocks of consecutive cards of the same suit (blocks may wrap past mark 20 to mark 1). The magician's rule: every maximal block must contain exactly 2 or exactly 3 cards. How many layouts obey the rule? Give your answer as an integer.

hints.text: Think of the rule as forcing the circle to be split into consecutive blocks of same-suit cards, each block having size 2 or 3, where consecutive blocks must have different suits (otherwise they'd merge into a bigger maximal run).

So the count splits into two independent tasks: (1) count the ways to partition the 20 labeled marks into a cyclic sequence of blocks of sizes 2 and 3, and (2) count the proper 3-colorings of the resulting cycle of blocks so adjacent blocks differ.

For part (1), find all combinations of block-counts $a$ of size 2 and $b$ of size 3 with $2a+3b=20$, giving total blocks $k=a+b$; for each $k$, the number of ways to cut the labeled circle into such blocks is $\frac{20}{k}\binom{k}{b}$. For part (2), recall that the number of proper 3-colorings of a cycle of length $k$ is $2^k+2(-1)^k$.

Compute both quantities for each valid $(a,b,k)$ pair — you should get $k=10,9,8,7$ with cutting counts $2,80,175,20$ and coloring counts $1026,510,258,126$ respectively — then multiply matching pairs and sum all four products to get the final total.

public.title: The Folding Duel

statement.final: At the origami club's grand finale, the judge slices a paper disc into a single sector, its angle n being a whole number of degrees chosen uniformly at random from 1 to 360. Alice and Bob then take turns folding, with Alice going first. Each fold works like this: the player picks a whole number d with 1 ≤ d < n, creases the sector along the radius sitting d degrees from one straight edge, and folds that d-degree sliver over the rest. The paper's outline becomes a new sector of max(d, n−d) degrees, and play continues on this new angle. Every fold strictly shrinks the angle, and it can never dip below 1°. Whoever is staring at a 1° sliver and cannot make a legal fold loses the duel. Both Alice and Bob are flawless strategists who always play optimally. Given the random draw of n and perfect play from both sides, what is the probability that Alice wins the folding duel? Give your answer as a fraction in lowest terms.
statement.original: At the origami club's finale, the judge cuts a paper disc into one sector whose angle is a whole number of degrees n, chosen uniformly at random from 1 to 360. Alice and Bob then alternate folds, Alice first. A fold works like this: pick a whole number d with 1 ≤ d < n, crease the sector along the radius that is d degrees from one of its straight edges, and fold that d-degree piece over. The outline is now a sector of max(d, n−d) degrees, which becomes the new angle. (So every fold strictly decreases the angle, and it can never go below 1°.) A player who cannot fold — that is, who faces a 1° sector — loses. Both play optimally. What is the probability that Alice wins? Give your answer as a fraction in lowest terms.

hints.text: Think about what set of angles a fold from n can actually reach in one move, rather than about a single d.

Notice that as d ranges over all legal choices, max(d,n-d) sweeps out a contiguous range of angles, so this is really a combinatorial game on integers where you classify each n as a win (W) or loss (L) for the player to move.
Work out small cases by hand — n=1,2,3,4,...,15 — labeling each L or W based on whether it can reach an L position, and watch for the special angles that are always L no matter what.
Show by induction that the L-positions are exactly n=2^k-1 (1,3,7,15,31,63,127,255), count how many of these lie between 1 and 360, and then use that count to get the win probability for Alice.

statement.final: The grand old Athenaeum has a reading floor laid out as a tidy grid of junctions: 3 rows and 4 columns of them. Between every pair of junctions that sit directly beside or above/below one another runs a straight corridor lined with bookshelves — 17 corridors in total connecting the whole floor. Tonight, after closing, the librarian must push her heavy reshelving cart down every single one of these 17 corridors at least once, since each is due for restocking. She may begin her round at whichever junction she likes and end at whichever junction she likes — the two need not match — and she's welcome to roll back and forth over the same corridor or through the same junction as many times as necessary to get the job done. Counting every time the cart rolls the full length of a corridor as one traversal (so going down the same corridor twice counts as two), she wants to plan the most efficient route possible before her coffee goes cold. What is the smallest possible total number of corridor-traversals needed to cover every corridor at least once? Give your answer as an integer.
statement.original:
The Athenaeum's reading floor is a 3-by-4 grid of junctions (3 rows, 4 columns). A straight corridor joins every pair of junctions that are horizontally or vertically adjacent, for 17 corridors in all; each corridor is lined with shelves.

Tonight the librarian must reshelve books, so her cart has to travel down every one of the 17 corridors at least once. She may start at any junction and finish at any junction (not necessarily the same one), and the cart may pass through junctions and corridors as often as she likes.

Counting one traversal each time the cart travels a corridor from end to end, what is the smallest possible total number of corridor-traversals in such a route?

Give your answer as an integer.

hints.text: Think about which junctions have an odd number of corridors meeting them — that parity structure is what determines whether a single continuous route can cover every corridor without repeats.

This is a route-inspection (Chinese postman) style problem: a route that uses every corridor exactly once from start to some end exists only if at most two junctions have odd degree, so you need to find how many junctions violate this and fix all but two of them by repeating corridors.

Work out the degree of every junction in the 3×4 grid (corners, edge-midpoints, interior points) and count how many are odd; then think about which pairs of these odd junctions are closest together, since repeating the corridor between a pair fixes both their parities cheaply.

Identify that there are 6 odd-degree junctions, so you must correct 4 of them via repeated corridors while leaving 2 as your start and end; find the two adjacent odd-degree pairs (top row and bottom row) whose connecting corridors you can double at minimal cost, then add that cost to the base 17 corridors.

public.title: Captain Mira's Buried Treasure

statement.final: Skull Island's map is a 5×5 grid of 25 distinct plots, each identified by its row and column. Captain Mira's crew has divided their plunder into three identical treasure chests, and old pirate superstition insists that when burying them, no two chests may end up in the same row, and no two chests may end up in the same column of the island. The chests themselves are indistinguishable from one another, so two burial plans are considered the same arrangement whenever the three chosen plots are exactly the same set of squares, regardless of which chest was buried where. Captain Mira wants to know, before she starts digging: how many genuinely different arrangements of the three buried chests satisfy the superstition's rules? Give your answer as an integer.
statement.original: Skull Island is divided into a 5×5 grid of 25 distinct plots, labeled by row and column. Captain Mira's crew splits the loot into three identical chests and buries them in three different plots. Superstition demands that no two chests share a row, and no two chests share a column. Since the chests are identical, two burials count as the same arrangement exactly when they occupy the same set of three plots. How many different arrangements of the three buried chests are possible? Give your answer as an integer.

hints.text: Think about what it really means for three plots to share no row and no column — it's about which rows and columns get used, not just individual squares.
The key idea: pick a subset of 3 rows and a subset of 3 columns first, then figure out how to pair them up into actual plots.
Count the number of ways to choose the 3 rows and the 3 columns separately (each a binomial choice from 5), and then think about how many ways there are to match up chosen rows with chosen columns.

You have $\binom{5}{3}$ ways to pick the rows and $\binom{5}{3}$ ways to pick the columns; now multiply by the number of bijections between the two size-3 sets, since each bijection gives a distinct valid set of three plots — combine these three counts to finish.

public.title: Ms. Ramirez's Perfect Schedule

statement.final: Ms. Ramirez is a beloved teacher who has exactly 18 lessons to squeeze into her week. The school week runs Monday through Friday, and each day is carved into six periods, numbered 1 through 6. The principal's job is to assign her 18 lessons to 18 distinct day/period slots — only which slots are used for teaching matters, not which specific lesson goes where. Ms. Ramirez has just one request, and it's a matter of personal comfort: she despises having an empty period trapped between two teaching periods on the same day. So for every day, whatever periods she teaches must form one unbroken, consecutive block — no gaps allowed. Of course, a day where she teaches nothing, or only one period, automatically makes her happy, since there's no way to sandwich a gap in those cases. Given this single, sensible rule, how many different weekly timetables could the principal create that would leave Ms. Ramirez completely satisfied? Give your answer as an integer.
statement.original: Ms. Ramirez teaches 18 lessons a week. The school week runs Monday through Friday, and every day has six periods, numbered 1 through 6. The principal assigns her 18 lessons to 18 distinct slots (day/period pairs); only the set of slots she teaches matters, not which lesson lands where. Her one request is the best possible arrangement for her: she never wants a free period sandwiched between two teaching periods on the same day, so on each day the periods she teaches must form a consecutive block. A day with no lessons, or with exactly one lesson, automatically satisfies this. How many different weekly timetables satisfy her request? Give your answer as an integer.

hints.text: Think about the problem one day at a time: since only slot occupancy matters, what really needs counting per day is the number of ways to place a consecutive block of taught periods (including possibly none), and then you need to combine five independent days so the totals add to 18.

Use generating functions: encode each day's possibilities as a polynomial where the coefficient of $x^k$ counts the ways to teach exactly $k$ consecutive periods that day, then the answer is a single coefficient in the fifth power of that polynomial.

Work out the per-day polynomial explicitly: a block of length $k\ge1$ among 6 periods can start in $7-k$ ways, plus 1 way for an empty day, giving $f(x)=1+6x+5x^2+4x^3+3x^4+2x^5+x^6$. You need the coefficient of $x^{18}$ in $f(x)^5$.

Build up the power step by step: first square $f$ to get its coefficients up to $x^{12}$, then multiply by $f$ again to get $f^3$'s coefficients up to $x^{18}$, and finally combine $f^3$ with $f^2$ by summing products of coefficients whose exponents add to 18 — carrying out this last convolution gives the final count.
